title: Australia’s biggest float: $50bn AI firm Firmus to dwarf Telstra
full_text:
Firmus is heading for a staggering $50bn market capitalisation if its planned listing on the ASX next month comes to fruition, as the artificial-intelligence data centre business defies global calls for AI development to slow down.
At current management projections, Firmus could pull off the biggest-ever valuation upon listing on the ASX, surpassing the $42bn market cap of Telstra with an expected value topping $50bn.
The AI neocloud firm, headed by billionaire Oliver Curtis and his co-founder cousin Tim Rosenfield, is seeking $US5bn ($7bn) from investors for its blockbuster initial public offering.
Its ASX float is set to be launched in about two weeks and take place towards the end of October.
Firmus management are promoting the company to Asian investors this week, before turning their attention to Melbourne and Sydney next week.
The valuation discussions come amid a call by Anthropic boss Dario Amodei for the pace of development of AI models to slow down and to be closely monitored. Rivals Sam Altman of OpenAI and Elon Musk, said they agreed with Mr Amodei.
Firmus last week signed OpenAI as a customer, turbocharging its valuation. The privately held company’s valuation has skyrocketed in the past year, making Mr Curtis and his father Nick billionaires on paper and providing big returns for early shareholders such as Phil King’s Regal, Alex Waislitz’s Thorney and Ashok Jacob’s Ellerston Capital, and more recent investors such as Wilson Asset Management and billionaires such as James Packer and Wes Maas.
The OpenAI pact lifts Firmus’ total capacity to 900 megawatts and stretches its operational reach across Malaysia, Singapore, Indonesia and Australia. Two small sites are already running, with five further factories expected to be delivered by the end of 2028.
The 900MW of compute contracted is estimated to be equivalent to $US41bn of capital spending, according to Wells Fargo estimates.
The imminent float will land during an unprecedented boom in data centre investment in Australia, with up to $200bn of deals amid a clamour by AI chipmakers for compute capacity.
Australia has 6 gigawatts of potential capacity in the pipeline, according to Fitch Ratings, although a clampdown by both federal and state governments on electricity and water use has changed the sector’s credit profile toward execution and financing risk.
Measures to keep a lid on household electricity bills, weakening grid reliability or slowing the energy transition have been drafted while big transmission providers like Transgrid have put their own policies in place to ensure data centre operators pay for new network costs.
New rules “would also require developers to take greater responsibility for renewable-energy sourcing, firming capacity, network augmentation and grid support”, Fitch said.
“Strong demand and limited supply in key markets may allow operators to recover part of these costs through customer contracts over time. Even so, developers would still face higher upfront funding requirements and execution risk.”
Transgrid forecasts demand from data centres will be four times higher than projected just one year ago.
Data centres will grow from 3 per cent of peak demand currently to 20 per cent by 2035.
Still, energy consultancy Rennie Advisory said solving the AI riddle in large part would come down to finding a solution for securing enough power supplies.
The growth of the global semiconductor market is roughly 56 per cent annually. Data centre power consumption is forecast to grow at 30 per cent a year while renewable generation is estimated to increase by 8 per cent over the same period.
Firmus was priced at $15.5bn in July after a capital raising that included funds contributed by Nvidia, private equity giant Blackstone, technology investment manager Coatue and the ASX’s Maas Group.
Mr Curtis and Mr Rosenfield have now clinched deals with three of the biggest AI companies in the world in Nvidia, OpenAI and Meta – which has not been officially named by Firmus, but is widely regarded as a customer.
